title: Ad Abolendam: Systematic Inquisition Against Heresy Begins
description: Pope Lucius III issued the decretal Ad Abolendam in 1184, establishing the first systematic inquisitorial framework for prosecuting heresy across the Western Church. The decretal required bishops to make regular circuits of their dioceses to identify and punish heretics, mandated cooperation between ecclesiastical and secular courts, and imposed standardized penalties. While aimed primarily at Cathar and Waldensian movements, Ad Abolendam created the institutional infrastructure — the episcopal inquisition — that would later be applied to witchcraft prosecution. The blending of ecclesiastical investigation with secular punishment established by this decretal was a crucial procedural precondition for the witch trials.
historiographical_note: Henry Charles Lea's foundational History of the Inquisition of the Middle Ages (1887) traced the institutional development from Ad Abolendam to the Papal Inquisition established under Gregory IX, showing how procedural machinery built for heresy prosecution was readily adapted for witchcraft. More recent scholars like Edward Peters have emphasized how the inquisitorial procedure's reliance on confession shaped what accusations produced.
source_method: Corpus Iuris Canonici; papal registers; secondary scholarship on the medieval inquisition
